SVD Contextual Sparsity Predictors for Fast LLM Inference

Georgii Serbin Affiliation: Huawei Technologies Ltd.    Kirill Koshkin Affiliation: Moscow State University, Russia    Zhongao Sun Affiliation: Huawei Technologies Ltd.    Anastasiya Bistrigova Affiliation: Huawei Technologies Ltd. Affiliation: Moscow State University, Russia    C.C. Korikov Affiliation: Huawei Technologies Ltd. Correspondence to: constantine.korikov@gmail.com
Abstract

Contextual sparsity is one of the approaches used to reduce computational complexity in the inference process of large language models (LLMs). Existing techniques for efficient LLM inference acceleration based on contextual sparsity with minimal accuracy degradation require training sparse pattern predictors. This paper presents a framework for accelerating inference of ReGLU-based feed-forward networks (FFNs) within LLMs. The proposed framework provides a fast, training-free method for building sparse pattern predictors using truncation-aware singular value decomposition (SVD) of the gate projection matrix, along with a threshold calibration algorithm, and inference executors supporting conditional computation on CUDA and CANN devices. Experiments on three sparse LLMs with an average activation sparsity level of 90% in the FFNs demonstrate up to a 1.8×\times reduction in end-to-end decoding time while maintaining less than 1% degradation in benchmark scores on tasks involving complex math and code generation. This work advances the deployment of LLMs on edge devices.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML, Large Language Models, Inference Acceleration, Contextual Sparsity, Activation Sparsity

1 Introduction

The remarkable capabilities of LLMs have led to their widespread integration across diverse domains (Brown et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2024b). While on-device AI deployment offers advantages in privacy, latency, and cost compared to server-based solutions (Shankar, 2024), the substantial computational requirements of LLM inference present significant challenges for edge deployment.

A key characteristic of ReGLU-based LLMs is dynamic (or contextual) sparsity – the phenomenon where only a small subset of neurons within FFN blocks are activated for any given input. This inherent property enables inference acceleration by reducing both computational overhead and memory bandwidth requirements during generation (Liu et al., 2023).

A prevalent approach for leveraging contextual sparsity involves employing lightweight, learnable sparsity predictors (Liu et al., 2023). These predictors generate input-specific sparse activation patterns prior to FFN forward passes. The sparse pattern identifies neuron indices that will produce positive dot products with the input vector. In ReGLU FFNs, computations for the remaining neurons can be safely skipped without affecting output correctness, as the activation function nullifies negative values. Nevertheless, prediction errors may arise from false negative classifications, which compromise model accuracy. Effective predictors must balance high recall rates with substantial sparsity ratios while maintaining sufficient speed to reduce end-to-end (E2E) text generation latency.

In this study, we present a simple yet effective technique leveraging low-rank singular value decomposition (SVD) to predict sparse patterns, thereby enabling significant inference acceleration in ReGLU-based LLMs. Our methodology employs low-rank approximations of gate projection weight matrices in each layer as lightweight predictors of the FFN block sparsity mask during generation. Unlike existing contextual sparsity prediction methods, our approach provides theoretical guarantees regarding prediction accuracy.

To enhance the accuracy of SVD-based predictors, we employ a combination of techniques:

  • •

    Calibrated bias. Direct application of SVD approximations as predictors results in notable accuracy degradation. However, we observe that SVD predictors exhibit strong separation capabilities. Introducing neuron-specific thresholds – implemented as bias terms – effectively mitigates this issue. These biases are calibrated offline using a custom greedy algorithm that does not require gradient computation.

  • •

    Data whitening technique. Given the predictor speed constraints, the rank must be significantly smaller than the hidden dimension. To improve prediction accuracy under these conditions, we apply truncation-aware data whitening (Wang et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025b; Yuan et al., 2025). This technique reduces Frobenius norm error by incorporating input activation statistics, requiring only a small calibration dataset.

Implementation-level optimizations further enhance inference speedup:

  • •

    Sequential computation of gate and up projections. Gate and up projections are computed sequentially, enabling further acceleration through early elimination of false positive predictions. After computing gate projections, falsely activated neurons are identified and excluded from subsequent up and down projections, thereby increasing sparsity levels in the final FFN stages.

  • •

    Inference executors. Our implementations support conditional computation on CUDA (NVIDIA Corporation, 2024) and CANN (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., b) devices. For CUDA, we employ custom kernels rather than Triton-based abstractions (Tillet et al., 2019), prioritizing enhanced low-level control. On Huawei Ascend hardware (Liao et al., 2019), comparable performance gains are achieved exclusively through high-level PyTorch APIs, demonstrating effective utilization of the platform’s native software stack.

Figure 1 illustrates our framework architecture.

Our key contributions are summarized as follows:

  1. 1.

    We propose training-free SVD-based contextual sparsity predictors for ReGLU-based LLM inference acceleration;

  2. 2.

    We introduce calibrated bias terms that significantly improve prediction accuracy, with biases tuned on small datasets using a custom gradient-free algorithm;

  3. 3.

    We develop executors supporting sparse FFN inference on CUDA and CANN devices;

  4. 4.

    We achieve up to 1.8×\times end-to-end inference speedup with minimal accuracy degradation.

2 Related Work

Sparsification is one of the most effective paradigms for accelerating LLM inference, typically categorized into static and dynamic sparsity methods.

Static sparsity removes redundant parameters before deployment (Ashkboos et al., 2024), reducing computation and memory costs but often sacrificing accuracy at high sparsity levels. In contrast, dynamic sparsity – also known as dynamic pruning or contextual sparsity – adapts sparsity patterns at runtime based on input context, enabling flexible efficiency-accuracy trade-offs.

Predictor-based dynamic sparsity methods, such as Deja Vu (Liu et al., 2023) and ShadowLLM (Akhauri et al., 2024), learn lightweight neural predictors to estimate layer-wise sparsity. ShadowLLM enhances this approach by incorporating gradient information during training and utilizing a single predictor for all layers.

Training-free dynamic sparsity eliminates learned predictors and instead derives sparsity from activation statistics or calibrated thresholds. GRIFFIN (Dong et al., 2024a) selects active “expert” neurons using prefill activations, while TDA (Ma et al., 2024) introduces offline-calibrated thresholds allowing adaptive activation per layer. Both maintain fixed sparsity patterns within a prompt. CLADA (Yang et al., 2025) updates sparsity during generation but requires recomputation of previous states, hindering KV-cache reuse. TEAL (Liu et al., 2024) exploits input sparsity, which differs from activation sparsity in that it arises from redundancy in the input representations rather than neuron activations, using calibrated thresholds. SparseInfer (Shin et al., 2025) proposes a calibrated solution for ReLU-fied LLMs using sign-bit comparisons, which lacks theoretical justifications.

Dynamic sparsity can also underpin efficient on-device inference frameworks. PowerInfer (Song et al., 2024b) accelerates LLMs on consumer GPUs by preloading frequently activated neurons into GPU memory, minimizing CPU transfers. It achieves up to 11.69×\times speedup, particularly in CPU/GPU hybrid settings, whereas our work targets homogeneous GPU inference with batch size one.

The effectiveness of dynamic sparsity depends heavily on activation functions. ReLU activations naturally induce sparse activations, unlike smoother functions such as Swish or SiLU used in modern LLMs (Zhang et al., 2024). Recent studies show that replacing them with ReLU variants plus fine-tuning recovers substantial sparsity (Mirzadeh et al., 2023). ProSparse (Song et al., 2024a) achieved ∼\sim90% sparsity in LLaMA2-7B through progressive regularization and activation threshold shifting, while TurboSparse (Song et al., 2024c) used double ReLU (dReLU) activation function to sparsify models like Qwen2-7B and Mistral-7B.

Beyond pruning, SVD offers complementary compression capabilities. ASVD (Yuan et al., 2025) leverages activation-aware transformations to attain 10–30% model compression, and SVD-LLM (Wang et al., 2025b) provides theoretical connections between discarded components and L2L_{2} loss.

SparseLoRA (Khaki et al., 2025) integrates SVD-based estimators into parameter-efficient fine-tuning, dynamically slicing weights by input relevance. However, sparse computations are applied only to context tokens (the prefix tokens provided as input), while output tokens (the target tokens used for loss computation) remain densely processed to avoid performance degradation. Achieving accelerated and high-quality decoding of LLMs through contextual sparsity remains an open challenge not addressed by SparseLoRA.

3 Preliminaries

Consider a ReGLU-activated FFN block during decoding, defined as:

FFN​(x)=Wdown​(ReLU​(Wgate​x)⊙(Wup​x)),\text{FFN}(x)=W^{\mathrm{down}}\left(\text{ReLU}(W^{\mathrm{gate}}x)\odot\left(W^{\mathrm{up}}x\right)\right), (1)

where x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the input activation vector, and Wgate,Wup∈ℝD×dW^{\mathrm{gate}},W^{\mathrm{up}}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d}, and Wdown∈ℝd×DW^{\mathrm{down}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times D} are the gate, up-projection, and down-projection matrices, respectively. Here, dd denotes the hidden size and DD the intermediate size. Let X∈ℝd×NX\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N} denote the hidden states of NN calibration tokens, and let rr denote the predictor rank. For brevity, we omit layer indices.

Our objective is to obtain a predictor PP that outputs a binary mask m=P⁡(x)∈{0,1}Dm=P(x)\in\{0,1\}^{D} over the DD intermediate neurons. This mask identifies active neurons by selecting the corresponding rows of WgateW^{\mathrm{gate}} and WupW^{\mathrm{up}}, together with their aligned columns of WdownW^{\mathrm{down}}, yielding sparse computation algebraically equivalent to the dense FFN due to ReLU sparsity.

4 SVD-Based Sparsity Predictors

This section introduces training-free SVD-based sparsity predictors (SVDP), designed for efficient inference in ReGLU-based LLMs. Our approach consists of two stages: an offline phase for predictor construction and an online phase for accelerated sparse inference.

4.1 Training-free Predictor Building

The predictors are constructed by approximating the gate projection matrix WgateW^{\mathrm{gate}} using a low-rank SVD decomposition. This approach offers a theoretical upper bound on local error (see Section A.1).

We propose predictors of the affine form

P⁡(x)=H⁡(A​B​x+b),P(x)=H(ABx+b), (2)

where H:ℝ→{0,1}H:\mathbb{R}\to\{0,1\} is the Heaviside step function applied element-wise. H⁡(z)=1H(z)=1 if z>0z>0 and 00 otherwise. The product A​BAB approximates WgateW^{\mathrm{gate}}, while bb adjusts per-neuron decision thresholds.

4.1.1 Data-Aware SVD-Based Factorization

To improve the accuracy of the SVD approximation, we adopt a data whitening technique. This minimizes the Frobenius norm error:

‖W​X−Ur​Σr​Vr⊤​X‖F\|WX-U_{r}\Sigma_{r}V_{r}^{\top}X\|_{F} (3)

on calibration data XX, by incorporating input statistics through a whitening matrix SS:

W\displaystyle W =(W​S)​S−1\displaystyle=(WS)S^{-1} (4)
=(U​Σ​V⊤)​S−1≈Ur​Σr​Vr⊤​S−1=A​B.\displaystyle=(U\Sigma V^{\top})S^{-1}\approx U_{r}\Sigma_{r}V_{r}^{\top}S^{-1}=AB.

We follow Wang et al. (2025b) in choosing SS as the Cholesky decomposition of X​X⊤XX^{\top}, which outperforms ASVD in terms of perplexity at low ranks, as shown in Table 2 of Yuan et al. (2025).

The predictor construction pipeline is described in Algorithm 1 and is performed independently for each layer. Throughout, we fix the predictor rank rr across layers (see Section E.3 for a discussion on rank selection).

4.1.2 Threshold Calibration

SVD-based sparsity predictors typically exhibit good separation between active and inactive neurons; however, naive thresholding (e.g., at zero) leads to substantial accuracy degradation. This effect arises from a shift in the predictor output distribution induced by truncation of singular value components, as illustrated in Figure 2.

To compensate for this distribution shift, a bias term is introduced in the second layer of the SVD-based predictor. The central problem is to calibrate this bias so as to achieve a prescribed sparsity level while limiting the associated accuracy loss. Simple schemes that tune thresholds to match a target sparsity, recall, or accuracy on a calibration set were empirically found to yield suboptimal trade-offs.

Instead, a fast greedy calibration algorithm, Algorithm 2, is employed that explicitly accounts for the heterogeneous impact of different neurons on model accuracy. From a computational standpoint, all neurons are equally valuable for acceleration, since pruning any neuron reduces the cost by the same amount, whereas their contributions to output accuracy differ substantially. Consequently, some neurons require high recall, whereas others can tolerate higher false-negative rates without noticeably affecting overall performance. Under certain conditions, our greedy algorithm is guaranteed to provide an optimal solution (see Section A.2).

Let s∈(0,1]s\in(0,1] denote the desired sparsity ratio, controlling the speed-accuracy trade-off (see Section E.3). For each neuron i∈[D]i\in[D], initialize τi←mint:wi(t)>0si(t)\tau_{i}\leftarrow\min\limits_{t:\ w_{i}^{(t)}>0}s_{i}^{(t)}. Then greedily increase sparsity by advancing the neuron with smallest incremental cost ∑j=1ηwi,(ki+j)\sum_{j=1}^{\eta}w_{i,(k_{i}+j)} until

1D​T∑i=1D∑t=1T𝟏[si(t)≤τi]≥s.\frac{1}{DT}\sum_{i=1}^{D}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{1}[s_{i}^{(t)}\leq\tau_{i}]\geq s.

The penalty Ci​(ki+η)−Ci​(ki)C_{i}(k_{i}+\eta)-C_{i}(k_{i}) proxies FFN output perturbation across η\eta samples. Fixed biases b=−τ∈ℝDb=-\tau\in\mathbb{R}^{D} are used during inference.

The proposed predictor is lightweight and data-efficient, requiring only few thousands of tokens for reliable construction and bias estimation. It is fast and memory-efficient, making it suitable for practical use in constrained settings.

4.2 Runtime Execution

We modify only the FFNs; the rest of the model remains unchanged. During inference, the prefill stage remains unchanged. At the decoding stage, we leverage CUDA and CANN executors for sparse FFN computation. Figure 3 illustrates the sparse inference pipeline, where speedup is determined by the token-dependent sparsity ratio.

Sparsity Prediction

Our predictor comprises two linear layers, requiring no specialized implementation. Deja Vu employs lookahead predictors to circumvent prediction latency. This is enabled via asynchronous computation, where predictor execution time is overlapped with data transfer from global memory or inter-process communication under tensor parallelism. However, such pipelining may be infeasible on certain hardware platforms (see Appendix B). Given our focus on local inference for edge deployment scenarios, similar to PowerInfer engine, our predictors are inserted at the beginning of each FFN and sequentially generate sparsity patterns for their respective gate projections.

Gate/up Execution Order

A prevalent optimization for efficient deployment of LLMs with gated FFNs involves parallelized execution of the gate and up projections. While effective in dense computation scenarios, this approach presents non-trivial challenges for local inference systems leveraging sparse activations. We delineate two distinct computational methodologies to address this:

  • •

    Parallel pipeline e.g., PowerInfer. A predictor first generates a sparsity mask, which is concurrently applied to independently compute both gate and up projections. This maintains identical sparsity levels across both projections during execution.

  • •

    Sequential pipeline e.g., SparseInfer and our approach. The gate and up projections are computed sequentially, eliminating false positives: neurons predicted as active are revalidated after gate projection computation, further increasing sparsity in subsequent projections.

Algorithmic Complexity

In our case, realized sparsity equals or exceeds the predicted sparsity ss by filtering erroneous predictions. Thanks to sequential pipeline, we can use more lightweight predictors that provide relatively low sparsity at the gate projection stage without compromising the FFN’s performance.

A dense FFN requires 3​d​D3dD multiplications (excluding element-wise product), whereas our sparse approach reduces this to:

r⁡(d+D)⏟predictor+d⁡(1−s)​D⏟gate+2​d​(1−s′)​D⏟up/down\underbrace{r(d+D)}_{\text{predictor}}+\underbrace{d(1-s)D}_{\mathrm{gate}}+\underbrace{2d(1-s^{\prime})D}_{\text{up/down}} (5)

where ss is the predicted sparsity and s′s^{\prime} the realized sparsity. For example, in ProSparse-LLaMA2-7B (Song et al., 2024a) (d=4096d\!=\!4096, D=11008D\!=\!11008, s=0.5s\!=\!0.5, s′=0.9s^{\prime}\!=\!0.9, r=256r\!=\!256), operations decrease by 3.8×\times. Note that hardware-level dynamic sparsity challenges prevent this from directly translating to wall-clock speedup.

Hardware platforms

CUDA and CANN devices are supported for sparse FFN inference. See implementation details in Appendix B.

5 Experimental Results

5.1 Experimental Setup

Hardware

A single consumer-grade NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU 11 1 All GPU-based experiments were conducted exclusively by authors affiliated with Moscow State University (Kirill Koshkin) without involvement of Huawei-affiliated researchers. Huawei-affiliated co-authors contributed solely to theoretical analysis, algorithm design and CANN performance evaluation. at the MSU Laboratory of Computer Engineering is used for both quality and performance evaluation. The inference is performed entirely on GPU.

For evaluation on NPU, a single Ascend 310P3 (Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd., a) device is used.

Software

We use the vLLM framework (Kwon et al., 2023), preferring it to the Transformers framework (Wolf et al., 2020) for the experiments, as it better reflects real-world deployment scenarios. Notably, we do not utilize any server-specific features of vLLM, such as tensor parallelism. Inference is performed in half precision, while predictor construction in the offline stage uses double precision.

Models

We evaluate our solution across three open-source sparse 7B language models: ProSparse-LLaMA2-7B (Song et al., 2024a) and two instruction-tuned models – SparseQwen2-7B and TurboSparse-Mistral-Instruct (Song et al., 2024c).

The instruction-tuned models incorporate double ReLU (dReLU) activation in their FFN layers:

FFN​(x)=Wdown​(ReLU​(Wgate​x)⊙ReLU​(Wup​x))\text{FFN}(x)\!=\!W^{\mathrm{down}}\!\left(\text{ReLU}\!\left(W^{\mathrm{gate}}x\right)\!\odot\!\text{ReLU}\!\left(W^{\mathrm{up}}x\right)\right) (6)
Quality Evaluation

We evaluate model performance using a diverse set of open-source benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, knowledge, and multilingual understanding: GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) (math reasoning), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) (code generation), ARC-E/ARC-C (Clark et al., 2018) (scientific and commonsense reasoning), TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017) (open-domain QA), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) (small Python tasks), BBH (Suzgun et al., 2022) (complex reasoning), and CMMLU (Li et al., 2024) (Chinese multi-task understanding).

We adopt the UltraEval framework (He et al., 2024), aligning with prior ProSparse evaluations, as the model shows compatibility issues with lm-eval-harness (Gao et al., 2024). All benchmarks use free-form generation rather than perplexity scoring to better reflect real-world LLM usage.

Performance Evaluation

Model performance is measured using the PyTorch profiler (Ansel et al., 2024). For each domain, results are averaged across multiple samples. E2E latency includes the prefill stage and 200-token generation.

5.2 Performance Under Different Sparsity Ratios

The desired sparsity hyperparameter ss from Algorithm 2 influences the calibrated thresholds and can be used to trade off accuracy and acceleration. As Table 1 shows, lower thresholds lead to lower sparsity and lower acceleration. In contrast, higher thresholds provide more speedup but may degrade quality. Long generation tasks are the most sensitive, while for short answer tasks the sparsity can be significantly increased. With our approach we can achieve up to 1.8×1.8\times E2E generation speedup while maintaining less than 1% degradation in benchmark scores on tasks involving complex math and code generation. See Appendix D for detailed evaluation results.

5.3 Comparison With Other Methods

We compare SVDP against training-free sparsity methods (GRIFFIN (Dong et al., 2024a)) and learnable predictors (PowerInfer (Song et al., 2024b), Deja Vu (Liu et al., 2023)). GRIFFIN relies on prompt-based statistical sparsity patterns, while PowerInfer and Deja Vu use trained predictors.

For Deja Vu, we trained predictors following their official repository instructions. For PowerInfer, we used their recommended pretrained predictors.

Benchmarks

Table 2 shows that our SVDP matches PowerInfer’s accuracy and sparsity while requiring less data and compute for construction. GRIFFIN struggles with stable performance at high sparsity ratios, particularly for long generations. The sequential pipeline implementation reduces SVDP size by 4×\times without compromising either accuracy or inference speed.

ROC-AUC Analysis

We also evaluate predictor separation ability via layer-wise ROC-AUC scores on held-out test sequences (Figure 4). SVDP outperforms learnable baselines on unseen data. Trained predictors may suffer from out-of-distribution sensitivity due to their data-dependent nature, while SVD predictors directly leverage the LLM’s internal weight structure.

5.4 Ablation Study

Table 3 shows ablation of SVD sparsity estimators, starting from SparseLoRA’s baseline (Khaki et al., 2025) (referred to as Naive SVD):

  • •

    Data whitening: Incorporate input data statistics (Sec. 4.1.1).

  • •

    Bias calibration: Add neuron-specific bias terms (Sec. 4.1.2).

Bias calibration significantly improves accuracy by accounting for distribution shift after low-rank approximation.

Data whitening substantially enhances ROC-AUC separation vs. Naive SVD on held-out test sequences (Figure 5), independent of bias calibration.

5.5 Inference Executors

Table 4 presents FFN performance of our CUDA and CANN executors across varying sparsity ratios. Here, we use Huawei’s Ascend 310P3 AI accelerator. Notably, we achieve comparable performance gains on the Ascend hardware using only high-level PyTorch APIs, eliminating the need for manual low-level instruction optimization. This result facilitates deeper exploration of contextual sparsity optimizations within the DaVinci architecture. It is worth noting that when the sparsity value approaches 90%, the L1 (Liao et al., 2019) cache hit rate reaches almost 100%, resulting in a significant speedup increase.

6 Limitations

  • •

    Our method targets sparse models where non-linear activation functions naturally produce significant zero-valued outputs. Extension to non-ReGLU-based architectures remains an important direction for future research. See Appendix C for detailed discussion.

  • •

    Batched processing inherently reduces sparsity levels, limiting achievable speedups and precluding the use of sparsity predictors during the prefill phase.

Conclusion

This paper introduces a training-free framework for accelerating the inference of ReGLU-based large language models through contextual sparsity exploitation. The proposed solution comprises two stages: (1) an offline calibration phase where sparsity predictors are constructed using data-aware truncated singular value decomposition of gate projection matrices with calibrated bias parameters, and (2) an online inference phase enabling efficient sparse LLM execution on CUDA and CANN devices. Evaluation across three sparse language models demonstrates up to 1.8×\times end-to-end decoding acceleration with minimal accuracy degradation across diverse benchmarks, including code and mathematical reasoning tasks.

Appendix A Theoretical Analysis

A.1 Predictor error bounds

Let m,d>0m,d>0 and 0<r≤min⁡(m,d)0<r\leq\min(m,d). Consider a weight matrix W∈ℝm×dW\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} and its rank-rr approximation Wr∈ℝm×dW_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} (e.g., truncated SVD), with bias vector b∈ℝmb\in\mathbb{R}^{m}. For any input x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, x≠0x\neq 0, we have:

A⁡(x)\displaystyle A(x) :=ReLU⁡(W​x),\displaystyle:=\operatorname{ReLU}(Wx), (7)
gb​(x)\displaystyle g_{b}(x) :=𝟏[Wrx+b>0],\displaystyle:=\mathbf{1}[W_{r}x+b>0], (8)
Bb​(x)\displaystyle B_{b}(x) :=A⁡(x)⊙gb​(x).\displaystyle:=A(x)\odot g_{b}(x). (9)

Throughout, we use the following notation:

δi\displaystyle\delta_{i} ∈ℝm,i∈[m],denotes the i-th standard basis vector (0,…,1⏟i,…,0)⊤,\displaystyle\in\mathbb{R}^{m},\quad i\in[m],\quad\text{denotes the $i$-th standard basis vector $(0,\ldots,\underbrace{1}_{i},\ldots,0)^{\top}$},
t+\displaystyle t_{+} :=max⁡(t,0),the ReLU function (i.e., t+=0 if t<0 and t+=t if t≥0).\displaystyle:=\max(t,0),\quad\text{the ReLU function (i.e., $t_{+}=0$ if $t<0$ and $t_{+}=t$ if $t\geq 0$)}.

We aim to derive deterministic bounds on the relative gating error

ℰb​(x):=‖A⁡(x)−Bb​(x)‖2‖x‖2\mathcal{E}_{b}(x):=\frac{\left\lVert A(x)-B_{b}(x)\right\rVert_{2}}{\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}}

in terms of the spectral error of WrW_{r} and the bias bb.

Exact error representation and monotonicity
Definition A.1 (Residual operator).

Define the residual matrix and residual vector

Δ​W:=W−Wr,e⁡(x):=Δ​W​x.\Delta W:=W-W_{r},\qquad e(x):=\Delta Wx.
Proposition A.2 (Exact representation of the gating error).

For every x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

A(x)−Bb(x)=ReLU(Wx)⊙𝟏[Wrx+b≤0],A(x)-B_{b}(x)=\operatorname{ReLU}(Wx)\odot\mathbf{1}[W_{r}x+b\leq 0], (10)

and therefore

‖A(x)−Bb(x)‖22=∑i=1m((Wx)i)+2 1[(Wrx+b)i≤0].\left\lVert A(x)-B_{b}(x)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left((Wx)_{i}\right)_{+}^{2}\,\mathbf{1}[(W_{r}x+b)_{i}\leq 0]. (11)
Proof.

The claim follows immediately from the componentwise definition of Bb​(x)B_{b}(x). ∎

Proposition A.3 (Monotonicity w.r.t. biases).

Let b,b′∈ℝmb,b^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and suppose b′≤bb^{\prime}\leq b componentwise. Then for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

‖A⁡(x)−Bb′​(x)‖2≥‖A⁡(x)−Bb​(x)‖2.\left\lVert A(x)-B_{b^{\prime}}(x)\right\rVert_{2}\;\geq\;\left\lVert A(x)-B_{b}(x)\right\rVert_{2}.
Proof.

If b′≤bb^{\prime}\leq b, then 𝟏[Wrx+b≤0]≤ 1[Wrx+b′≤0]\mathbf{1}[W_{r}x+b\leq 0]\ \leq\ \mathbf{1}[W_{r}x+b^{\prime}\leq 0] componentwise. Using the identity (10) and the fact that ReLU⁡(W​x)≥0\operatorname{ReLU}(Wx)\geq 0 componentwise, the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm can only increase when we replace bb by the smaller bias b′b^{\prime}, which activates the mask on a superset of coordinates. ∎

Remark A.4.

Using thresholds τ=−b\tau=-b clarifies the trade-off: increasing τ\tau increases sparsity (more gates are off) but never decreases the error; equivalently, increasing bb reduces sparsity and never increases the error.

A deterministic bound via the shifted residual
Lemma A.5 (Residual-based upper bound).

For every x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and b∈ℝmb\in\mathbb{R}^{m},

‖A⁡(x)−Bb​(x)‖2≤‖(Δ​W​x−b)+‖2≤‖Δ​W​x−b‖2.\left\lVert A(x)-B_{b}(x)\right\rVert_{2}\;\leq\;\left\lVert\left(\Delta Wx-b\right)_{+}\right\rVert_{2}\;\leq\;\left\lVert\Delta Wx-b\right\rVert_{2}. (12)
Proof.

Let z=W​xz=Wx, zr=Wr​xz_{r}=W_{r}x, and e:=z−zr=Δ​W​xe:=z-z_{r}=\Delta Wx. Define the gated index set

I:={i∈[m]:(zr+b)i≤0}.I:=\{i\in[m]:(z_{r}+b)_{i}\leq 0\}.

By definition,

‖A⁡(x)−Bb​(x)‖22=∑i∈I(zi)+2.\left\lVert A(x)-B_{b}(x)\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\sum_{i\in I}\left(z_{i}\right)_{+}^{2}.

For i∈Ii\in I we have zr,i≤−biz_{r,i}\leq-b_{i}, hence zi=zr,i+ei≤ei−biz_{i}=z_{r,i}+e_{i}\leq e_{i}-b_{i}. By monotonicity of t↦(t)+t\mapsto\left(t\right)_{+}, (zi)+≤(ei−bi)+\left(z_{i}\right)_{+}\leq\left(e_{i}-b_{i}\right)_{+}. Therefore

∑i∈I(zi)+2≤∑i=1m(ei−bi)+2=‖(e−b)+‖22,\sum_{i\in I}\left(z_{i}\right)_{+}^{2}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(e_{i}-b_{i}\right)_{+}^{2}=\left\lVert\left(e-b\right)_{+}\right\rVert_{2}^{2},

which gives the first inequality. The second inequality follows from ‖(u)+‖2≤‖u‖2\left\lVert\left(u\right)_{+}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{2}. ∎

Worst-case bounds

Due to the previous result, the analysis of the nonlinear gating error reduces to a deterministic quantity depending only on the residual Δ​W​x\Delta Wx and the bias bb. We therefore can study the worst-case value

sup‖e‖2≤R‖(e−b)+‖2,\sup_{\left\lVert e\right\rVert_{2}\leq R}\left\lVert\left(e-b\right)_{+}\right\rVert_{2},

which characterizes the maximal gating error at residual energy RR.

Uniform bias
Theorem A.6 (Worst-case bound for uniform bias).

Let b=β​𝟏b=\beta\mathbf{1} with β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R}. For all R≥0R\geq 0,

sup‖e‖2≤R‖(e−β​𝟏)+‖2={(R−β)+,β≥0,R−β​m,β<0.\sup_{\left\lVert e\right\rVert_{2}\leq R}\left\lVert\left(e-\beta\mathbf{1}\right)_{+}\right\rVert_{2}=\begin{cases}\left(R-\beta\right)_{+},&\beta\geq 0,\\[3.0pt] R-\beta\sqrt{m},&\beta<0.\end{cases}

Case 1: β≥0\beta\geq 0. Write y:=(e−β​𝟏)+∈ℝ≥0my:=\left(e-\beta\mathbf{1}\right)_{+}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{\geq 0} and t:=‖y‖2t:=\left\lVert y\right\rVert_{2}.

‖e‖22≥∑i∈S(β+yi)2=β2​|S|+2​β​∑i∈Syi+∑i∈Syi2.\left\lVert e\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\;\geq\;\sum_{i\in S}(\beta+y_{i})^{2}\;=\;\beta^{2}|S|+2\beta\sum_{i\in S}y_{i}+\sum_{i\in S}y_{i}^{2}.

Since y≥0y\geq 0, we have ∑i∈Syi=‖y‖1≥‖y‖2=t\sum_{i\in S}y_{i}=\left\lVert y\right\rVert_{1}\geq\left\lVert y\right\rVert_{2}=t, and also |S|≥1|S|\geq 1. Therefore

‖e‖22≥β2+2​β​t+t2=(t+β)2,\left\lVert e\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\;\geq\;\beta^{2}+2\beta t+t^{2}\;=\;(t+\beta)^{2},

so ‖e‖2≥t+β\left\lVert e\right\rVert_{2}\geq t+\beta. Under ‖e‖2≤R\left\lVert e\right\rVert_{2}\leq R this yields t≤R−βt\leq R-\beta, i.e., ‖(e−β​𝟏)+‖2≤(R−β)+\left\lVert\left(e-\beta\mathbf{1}\right)_{+}\right\rVert_{2}\leq(R-\beta)_{+}.

Equality holds by taking

R≤β:\displaystyle R\leq\beta: e=0,\displaystyle\quad e=0,
R>β:\displaystyle R>\beta: e=R​δ1.\displaystyle\quad e=R\delta_{1}.

Case 2: β<0\beta<0. Write β=−c\beta=-c with c>0c>0. Then for any ee,

‖(e−β​𝟏)+‖2=‖(e+c​𝟏)+‖2≤‖e+c​𝟏‖2≤‖e‖2+c​‖𝟏‖2≤R+c​m=R−β​m.\left\lVert\left(e-\beta\mathbf{1}\right)_{+}\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\left(e+c\mathbf{1}\right)_{+}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert e+c\mathbf{1}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert e\right\rVert_{2}+c\left\lVert\mathbf{1}\right\rVert_{2}\leq R+c\sqrt{m}=R-\beta\sqrt{m}.

Equality holds for e=Rm​𝟏e=\frac{R}{\sqrt{m}}\mathbf{1}. ∎

General bias vector
Theorem A.7 (Worst-case bound for general bias).

Let b∈ℝmb\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and R≥0R\geq 0. Then

sup‖e‖2≤R‖(e−b)+‖2={maxi∈[m]⁡(R−bi)+,b≥0​componentwise,R+‖b‖2,b<0​componentwise.\sup_{\left\lVert e\right\rVert_{2}\leq R}\left\lVert\left(e-b\right)_{+}\right\rVert_{2}=\begin{cases}\max_{i\in[m]}(R-b_{i})_{+},&b\geq 0\;\;\text{componentwise},\\[10.00002pt] R+\left\lVert b\right\rVert_{2},&b<0\;\;\text{componentwise}.\end{cases}
Proof.

Case 1: b<0b<0.

‖(e−b)+‖2≤‖e−b‖2≤R+‖b‖2.\left\lVert(e-b)_{+}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert e-b\right\rVert_{2}\leq R+\left\lVert b\right\rVert_{2}.

Tightness: e=R‖b‖2​(−b)e=\frac{R}{\left\lVert b\right\rVert_{2}}(-b) gives exactly R+‖b‖2R+\left\lVert b\right\rVert_{2}.

Case 2: b≥0b\geq 0. For i⋆=arg⁡mini⁡bii^{\star}=\arg\min_{i}b_{i}, let bc=bi⋆​𝟏b_{c}=b_{i^{\star}}\mathbf{1}. Then (e−b)+≤(e−bc)+(e-b)_{+}\leq(e-b_{c})_{+} componentwise, so

‖(e−b)+‖2≤‖(e−bc)+‖2​≤(A.6)​(R−bi⋆)+=maxi⁡(R−bi)+.\left\lVert(e-b)_{+}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left\lVert(e-b_{c})_{+}\right\rVert_{2}\overset{\eqref{thm:const_bias}}{\leq}(R-b_{i^{\star}})_{+}=\max_{i}(R-b_{i})_{+}.

Tightness: e=R​δi⋆e=R\delta_{i^{\star}} for i⋆=arg⁡maxi⁡(R−bi)+i^{\star}=\arg\max_{i}(R-b_{i})_{+} achieves equality. ∎

Remark A.8.

Theorem A.7 identifies two regimes in which the worst-case residual can be characterized exactly: a fully negative bias, where the bound grows linearly with ‖b−‖2\|b_{-}\|_{2}, and a fully nonnegative bias, where the optimum concentrates on a single coordinate.

Corollary A.9 (Main deterministic bound).

Let b∈ℝmb\in\mathbb{R}^{m} and R≥0R\geq 0 be such that ‖Δ​W​x‖2≤R\|\Delta Wx\|_{2}\leq R. Then for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

ℰb​(x)=‖A⁡(x)−Bb​(x)‖2‖x‖2≤{maxi∈[m]⁡(R−bi)+‖x‖2,b≥0​componentwise,R+‖b‖2‖x‖2,b<0​componentwise.\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)=\frac{\left\lVert A(x)-B_{b}(x)\right\rVert_{2}}{\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}}\leq\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\max_{i\in[m]}(R-b_{i})_{+}}{\|x\|_{2}},&b\geq 0\;\;\text{componentwise},\\[7.5pt] \displaystyle\frac{R+\|b\|_{2}}{\|x\|_{2}},&b<0\;\;\text{componentwise}.\end{cases}
Corollary A.10 (Truncated SVD).

By Eckart–Young–Mirsky, if WrW_{r} is the rank-rr truncated SVD of WgateW^{\mathrm{gate}}, then ‖Δ​W‖2=σr+1​(Wgate)=σr+1\|\Delta W\|_{2}=\sigma_{r+1}(W^{\mathrm{gate}})=\sigma_{r+1}, so for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

ℰb​(x)≤{maxi∈[m]⁡(σr+1−bi‖x‖2)+,b≥0​componentwise,σr+1+‖b‖2‖x‖2,b<0​componentwise.\mathcal{E}_{b}(x)\leq\begin{cases}\displaystyle\max_{i\in[m]}\left(\sigma_{r+1}-\frac{b_{i}}{\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}}\right)_{+},&b\geq 0\;\;\text{componentwise},\\[7.5pt] \displaystyle\sigma_{r+1}+\frac{\left\lVert b\right\rVert_{2}}{\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}},&b<0\;\;\text{componentwise}.\end{cases}
Remark A.11.

While rather loose in practice due to data distribution, this bound cleanly separates approximation error σr+1\sigma_{r+1} from gating bias bb, revealing bias addition’s influence on residuals.

A.2 Greedy threshold selection

Greedy threshold calibration under a fixed sparsity budget

We study a data-dependent calibration rule for componentwise thresholds τ∈ℝm\tau\in\mathbb{R}^{m} under a fixed drop budget KK (equivalently, fixed sparsity). Throughout, the gate is

gτ(x)=𝟏[ABx>τ],g_{\tau}(x)=\mathbf{1}[ABx>\tau],

where A​BAB denotes any rank-rr approximation of Wgate∈ℝm×dW^{\mathrm{gate}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}; the specific choice used in our experiments is given in Section 4.1.1.

Proxy scores and damage weights

Let 𝒟={x(t)}t=1T\mathcal{D}=\{x^{(t)}\}_{t=1}^{T} be a dataset and write [m]={1,…,m}[m]=\{1,\dots,m\}, [T]={1,…,T}[T]=\{1,\dots,T\}. For each coordinate i∈[m]i\in[m] and sample t∈[T]t\in[T] define the proxy score

si(t):=(A​B​x(t))i,s_{i}^{(t)}:=(ABx^{(t)})_{i},

and define the marginal damage weight

wi(t):=|ReLU(Wi,:gatex(t))⋅Wi,:upx(t)|2‖W:,idown‖22(≥0).w_{i}^{(t)}:=\left|\mathrm{ReLU}\left(W^{\mathrm{gate}}_{i,:}x^{(t)}\right)\cdot W^{\mathrm{up}}_{i,:}x^{(t)}\right|^{2}\left\|W^{\mathrm{down}}_{:,i}\right\|_{2}^{2}\qquad(\geq 0). (13)

Given thresholds τ\tau, the empirical output error incurred by dropping (i,t)(i,t) whenever si(t)≤τis_{i}^{(t)}\leq\tau_{i} is

ℒ(τ)=∑t=1T∑i=1mwi(t) 1[si(t)≤τi].\mathcal{L}(\tau)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_{i}^{(t)}\;\mathbf{1}[s_{i}^{(t)}\leq\tau_{i}]. (14)
Remark A.12 (Origin of the weight (13)).

Consider the standard gated FFN decomposition

z⁡(x)=ReLU⁡(Wgate​x)⊙(Wup​x),h⁡(x)=Wdown​z​(x).z(x)=\operatorname{ReLU}(W^{\mathrm{gate}}x)\odot(W^{\mathrm{up}}x),\qquad h(x)=W^{\mathrm{down}}z(x).

Then h⁡(x)h(x) decomposes into rank-one terms:

h(x)=∑i=1mzi(x)W:,idown,zi(x)=ReLU(Wi,:gatex)⋅Wi,:upx.h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_{i}(x)\,W^{\mathrm{down}}_{:,i},\quad z_{i}(x)=\operatorname{ReLU}(W^{\mathrm{gate}}_{i,:}x)\cdot W^{\mathrm{up}}_{i,:}x.

Dropping the ii-th hidden coordinate removes exactly the contribution vi(x)=zi(x)W:,idownv_{i}(x)=z_{i}(x)W^{\mathrm{down}}_{:,i}, hence

∥vi(x)∥22=|ReLU(Wi,:gatex)⋅Wi,:upx|2‖W:,idown‖22,\|v_{i}(x)\|_{2}^{2}=\left|\mathrm{ReLU}\left(W^{\mathrm{gate}}_{i,:}x\right)\cdot W^{\mathrm{up}}_{i,:}x\right|^{2}\left\|W^{\mathrm{down}}_{:,i}\right\|_{2}^{2},

which matches (13) for x=x(t)x=x^{(t)}.

Prefix formulation and fixed drop budget

Fix i∈[m]i\in[m]. Sort samples in nondecreasing order of proxy scores:

si,(1)≤si,(2)≤⋯≤si,(T),s_{i,(1)}\leq s_{i,(2)}\leq\cdots\leq s_{i,(T)},

and let wi,(j)w_{i,(j)} denote the corresponding permuted weights. Define

Ci​(k):=∑j=1kwi,(j),Ci​(0)=0,Δi​(k):=Ci​(k)−Ci​(k−1)=wi,(k).C_{i}(k):=\sum_{j=1}^{k}w_{i,(j)},\quad C_{i}(0)=0,\qquad\Delta_{i}(k):=C_{i}(k)-C_{i}(k-1)=w_{i,(k)}.

For each coordinate ii, setting τi\tau_{i} so exactly kik_{i} samples satisfy si(t)≤τis_{i}^{(t)}\leq\tau_{i} incurs cost Ci​(ki)C_{i}(k_{i}). The total loss is thus

ℒ⁡(τ)=∑i=1mCi​(ki),ki:=#⁡{t:si(t)≤τi}∈{0,…,T}.\mathcal{L}(\tau)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}C_{i}(k_{i}),\qquad k_{i}:=\#\{t:\ s_{i}^{(t)}\leq\tau_{i}\}\in\{0,\dots,T\}.

With fixed drop budget K∈{0,1,…,m​T}K\in\{0,1,\dots,mT\}, threshold selection reduces to

min⁡∑i=1mki∈{0,…,T}∑i=1mki=K⁡Ci​(ki).\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}k_{i}\in\{0,\dots,T\}\\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}k_{i}=K\end{subarray}}\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}C_{i}(k_{i}). (15)
Greedy optimality
Definition A.13 (Global optimality).

A feasible solution k⋆=(k1⋆,…,km⋆)k^{\star}=(k_{1}^{\star},\dots,k_{m}^{\star}) with ∑iki⋆=K\sum_{i}k_{i}^{\star}=K is globally optimal for (15) if

∑i=1mCi​(ki⋆)≤∑i=1mCi​(ki)for all feasible k=(k1,…,km).\sum_{i=1}^{m}C_{i}(k_{i}^{\star})\leq\sum_{i=1}^{m}C_{i}(k_{i})\quad\text{for all feasible $k=(k_{1},\dots,k_{m})$.}
Assumption A.14 (Monotone marginals within each coordinate).

For every i∈[m]i\in[m], the marginal increments are nondecreasing:

Δi​(1)≤Δi​(2)≤⋯≤Δi​(T).\Delta_{i}(1)\leq\Delta_{i}(2)\leq\cdots\leq\Delta_{i}(T).
Theorem A.15 (Greedy is globally optimal).

Initialize ki=0k_{i}=0 for all ii. For ℓ=1,2,…,K\ell=1,2,\dots,K (drop budget) choose

iℓ∈argmini:ki<TΔi(ki+1),and updatekiℓ←kiℓ+1.i_{\ell}\in\arg\min_{i:\,k_{i}<T}\ \Delta_{i}(k_{i}+1),\qquad\text{and update}\qquad k_{i_{\ell}}\leftarrow k_{i_{\ell}}+1.

Under Assumption A.14 the resulting kk is globally optimal for (15).

Moreover, it can be realized by thresholds τ\tau via

τi∈[si,(ki),si,(ki+1)),\tau_{i}\in[\,s_{i,(k_{i})},\,s_{i,(k_{i}+1)}\,),

with conventions si,(0):=−∞s_{i,(0)}:=-\infty and si,(T+1):=+∞s_{i,(T+1)}:=+\infty.

Proof.

The problem is equivalent to selecting exactly KK increments Δi​(j)\Delta_{i}(j) while respecting prefix constraints: selecting Δi​(j)\Delta_{i}(j) requires all Δi​(1),…,Δi​(j−1)\Delta_{i}(1),\dots,\Delta_{i}(j-1).

The greedy algorithm selects the smallest available “next increment” Δi​(ki+1)\Delta_{i}(k_{i}+1) at each step. Let GG be greedy’s sequence of KK increments, and OO any optimal sequence.

Suppose G≠OG\neq O. Let a=Δp​(kp+1)a=\Delta_{p}(k_{p}+1) be the first (chronologically) greedy increment not in OO. Since |G|=|O|=K|G|=|O|=K, there exists b=Δq​(j)∈O∖Gb=\Delta_{q}(j)\in O\setminus G.

Choose bb as the last increment of coordinate qq in OO (maximal jj). Removing bb preserves qq’s prefix constraint. Adding aa extends pp’s prefix, also preserving feasibility.

By greedy choice, a≤Δq​(kq+1)a\leq\Delta_{q}(k_{q}+1) where kqk_{q} counts greedy’s selections in qq up to that point. Since b∉Gb\notin G but OO includes it, j≥kq+1j\geq k_{q}+1. By Assumption A.14 (nondecreasing increments), Δq​(kq+1)≤Δq​(j)=b\Delta_{q}(k_{q}+1)\leq\Delta_{q}(j)=b.

Thus a≤ba\leq b, so swapping b↔ab\leftrightarrow a preserves feasibility and does not increase cost. Repeating such exchanges transforms OO into GG, proving optimality.

The threshold realization follows from the definition of kik_{i}. ∎

Remark A.16 (Role of rank-rr approximation and empirical validation).

Theorem A.15 requires monotone marginal increments after sorting by proxy scores (Assumption A.14). This is not guaranteed, since proxy scores si(t)=(A​B​x(t))is_{i}^{(t)}=(ABx^{(t)})_{i} depend only on rank-rr approximation A​B≈WgateAB\approx W^{\mathrm{gate}}, while damage, defined above, also involves WupW^{\mathrm{up}} and WdownW^{\mathrm{down}}.

If A​BAB approximates WgateW^{\mathrm{gate}} well on the input data distribution, then (A​B​x)i≈(Wgate​x)i(ABx)_{i}\approx(W^{\mathrm{gate}}x)_{i}, so proxy sorting should align with true damage ordering. In practice, we perform greedy selection over non-overlapping η\eta-step sums to mitigate data noise:

Si(m):=∑j=(m−1)​η+1m​ηwi,(j),m=1,…,⌊T/η⌋.S_{i}^{(m)}:=\sum_{j=(m-1)\eta+1}^{m\eta}w_{i,(j)},\quad m=1,\dots,\lfloor T/\eta\rfloor.

We validate their monotonicity using normalized Kendall tau distance between group sums and their position indices:

τiK:=1−Kd​({Si(m)}m=1M,{m}m=1M)M⁡(M−1),\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{K}}:=1-\frac{K_{d}\bigl(\{S_{i}^{(m)}\}_{m=1}^{M},\ \{m\}_{m=1}^{M}\bigr)}{M(M-1)},

where Kd(τ1,τ2)=#{(m1,m2):m1<m2,[τ1(m1)≶τ1(m2)∧τ2(m1)≷τ2(m2)]}K_{d}(\tau_{1},\tau_{2})=\#\bigl\{(m_{1},m_{2}):\ m_{1}<m_{2},\ [\tau_{1}(m_{1})\lessgtr\tau_{1}(m_{2})\land\tau_{2}(m_{1})\gtrless\tau_{2}(m_{2})]\bigr\} counts discordant pairs.

The use of Kendall tau distance is justified by the fact that it directly quantifies ordinal consistency required by Assumption A.14: for all m1<m2m_{1}<m_{2}, we expect Si(m1)≤Si(m2)S_{i}^{(m_{1})}\leq S_{i}^{(m_{2})}. Formally, τiK\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{K}} measures the fraction of concordant pairs while properly accounting for ties – the precise condition for greedy optimality in Theorem A.15. On sample data used to calibrate biases, Figure 6 shows stable Kendall τiK\tau_{i}^{\mathrm{K}} in [0.9,1][0.9,1], confirming proxy sorting A​B​x≈Wgate​xABx\approx W^{\mathrm{gate}}x and the suitability of our greedy approach.

Remark A.17 (Knapsack reformulation and practical optimality).

Problem (15) is a 00–11 knapsack problem with m​TmT items {Δi(j)}i=1mTj=1\{\Delta_{i}(j)\}_{i=1}^{m}{}_{j=1}^{T}, capacity KK, and prefix constraints that selection of Δi​(j)\Delta_{i}(j) requires prior selection of Δi​(1),…,Δi​(j−1)\Delta_{i}(1),\dots,\Delta_{i}(j-1). While standard dynamic programming requires O⁡(m​T​K)O(mTK) time, our greedy algorithm runs in O⁡((K+m)​log⁡m)O((K+m)\log m) via priority queue and is exactly optimal under Assumption A.14, yielding superior efficiency.

Appendix B Sparse FFN Inference Implementation

Unlike Deja Vu’s (Liu et al., 2023) asynchronous pipeline, which leverages Ampere’s cuda::memcpy_async operations (NVIDIA Corporation, 2024), our approach targets consumer-grade GPUs with compute capability 7.0 for broader applicability. Predictors are inserted at the beginning of each FFN and sequentially generate sparsity patterns for their respective gate projections. This design ensures minimal integration overhead with existing frameworks.

Custom CUDA Kernels for Sparse FFN

We implement three CUDA kernels (Algorithm 3).

The predictor’s output m∈ℝDm\in\mathbb{R}^{D} highlights active rows of WgateW^{\mathrm{gate}}. Throughout gate and up projections each CUDA block processes one neuron, first verifying its activity via mm. Gate outputs are stored back into mm for reuse. Key optimizations:

  • •

    Memory: Column-major storage of WdownW^{\mathrm{down}} for coalesced memory access.

  • •

    Precision: Full precision register operations; half precision for memory reads and writes.

  • •

    Determinism: Avoid atomic additions via shared-memory partial sums in down projection.

Our kernel design diverges from existing ProSparse (Song et al., 2024a) and Deja Vu (Liu et al., 2023) implementations. Both prior approaches rely on atomic addition operations within the down projection phase, introducing non-determinism and potential precision instability during floating-point accumulation. To address these limitations, our algorithm employs partial sum reduction implemented via shared memory. This technique enforces a predefined summation order and utilizes a hierarchical reduction strategy. Consequently, our approach guarantees deterministic outputs while simultaneously achieving enhanced numerical stability through reduced computational error propagation. We postpone kernel fusion due to diminishing returns, prioritizing maintainability.

NPU Solution for Sparse FFN

We implement our NPU solution for sparse FFN, detailed in Algorithm 4, leveraging high-level PyTorch instructions.

The predictor’s output m∈ℝDm\in\mathbb{R}^{D} is used to construct smaller dense submatrices by retrieving the corresponding rows or columns. This approach enables highly efficient execution by utilizing the dedicated matrix multiplication accelerator unit (cube) inherent to the CANN NPU architecture (Liao et al., 2019). WdownW^{\mathrm{down}} matrix is stored in column-major format.

Appendix C Extension to Non-ReLU Activations

The solution can in principle be applied to LLMs with non-ReLU activation functions, such as SiLU. However, the straightforward utilization may lead to substantial accuracy degradation on long generation tasks. The quality evaluation results for Qwen2-7B-Instruct model with SiLU activation function are presented at Table 5. Potential modifications to the current solution may include transformations to the intermediate activations to mitigate errors that arise.

Table 6, Table 7, Table 8 provide detailed evaluation results for three sparse LLMs equipped with our SVD-predictors.

Appendix E Technical details

E.1 LLMs hyperparameter values

We provide hyperparameter values for the tested models in Table 12, as they influence E2E latency. Specifically, all evaluated optimization techniques modify only the FFN portion of inference, leaving the attention block unchanged. Thus, a higher intermediate size increases the FFN’s contribution to E2E latency. Similarly, the use of Grouped Query Attention reduces the attention contribution to total inference time.

E.2 Predictor Building

For calibration in total we use 112 few-shot samples (≈\approx20000 tokens) from the train splits of the GSM8K, ARC-E, ARC-C, OpenBookQA, QAsper, CodeXGLUE datasets.

E.3 Predictor’s rank

One can trade off between the predicted sparsity ratio and predictor size. While a larger predictor allows for more sparse computations within gate projection, it requires more compute for prediction. In turn, the ss hyperparameter can be used to calibrate the predicted sparsity ratio. Figure 7 shows how the separation capability of SVD predictors depends on their size.

Due to this insight, higher acceleration can be achieved with relatively small predictors. Moreover, small predictors consume less additional memory. Similarly to rr, we set ss to be constant across all layers. Empirically, we found that setting the rank to approximately 2% of the intermediate size DD works well.
